newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - CWS continues legal barrage despite bid flop.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - CWS continues legal barrage despite bid flop.

text.p: Entrepreneur Andrew Regan gave up his ambitious plan to take over Britain's Co-operative Wholesale Society (CWS) on Thursday, but now faces further CWS legal action.
Regan's special bidding company, the Galileo Group, issued a brief statement saying it had abandoned its proposal to turn mutually-owned CWS into a limited company and then make a bid.

But the news has not taken any of the heat out of the war-of-words waged by the 153-year-old supermarkets to funeral parlours group which said it would begin a private prosecution against Regan and business associate David Lyons.

It also said it would begin proceedings against suspended CWS manager Allan Green for alleged theft of documents linked to the bid. And British merchant bank Hambros and law firm Travers Smith Braithwaite will also face a CWS civil action.
None of the parties were available for comment.

In another flurry of letters from CWS chief executive Graham Melmoth, he questioned Hambros chairman Lord Hambro over the exchange of papers. "It is inconceiveable that anyone could have concluded that the documents had been obtained by legitimate means from a legitimate source," he said.
It also emerged that British retailer Sainsbury had been in talks with Regan about buying some of the larger CWS properties.

But in a letter to the Co-op's lawyers, Sainsbury said it had obtained assurances from Galileo's adviser Hambros that all the information it had received "had been obtained without impropriety" and it had been returned.

Galileo said it would not pursue its bid after CWS chairman Lennox Fyfe on Wednesday rejected a plea for an end to legal proceedings and an invitation to put Galileo's plans to CWS members. Fyfe also instructed CWS directors to hand Galileo's proposals back "unopened and unread".

"In the light of this response, Galileo announces that it will not be pursuing its proposal," it said. But banking sources said the bid may have been withdrawn because one of the backers, Japanese securities giant Nomura Securities Co Ltd, had thought again following the allegations surrounding the main protagonists.
Regan has been stalking the Co-op for several months but an expected 1.2 billion pound ($1.9 billion) bid was thwarted by CWS legal action.

This resulted from CWS hiring private investigators to film Regan, his business associate Lyons and suspended CWS manager Allan Green. On Wednesday Regan and his team handed back a total of seven boxes of documents which Galileo said had been passed to it voluntarily by a CWS employee.

Galileo's apparent climb-down follows a high-profile and aggressive defence by CWS involving a High Court injunction and CWS making its concerns about a payment in a previous deal with Regan known to Britain's Serious Fraud Office.

CWS has interests ranging from farms and opticians to the profitable Co-operative Bank and a large insurance arm. Galileo's plan was widely reported to be to sell-off the CWS assets to unlock what one banking source described as "hidden value".
Galileo, an offshoot of 31-year-old Regan's Guernsey-based investment trust Lanica, had the backing of key City institutions including Nomura.

Its interest in CWS first became public in February and led to the suspension of Lanica's shares on the London Stock Exchange at 19.37 pounds. The shares were star performers last year, rising from 203 pence when Regan took over.
Banking sources said the Stock Exchange would be meeting with Lanica to discuss relisting the shares, but this was not expected to take place imminently.

Despite its poorly performing retail business, CWS has consistently rejected any suggestion of selling any of its businesses to Regan or anyone else. The group's complex structure has also been seen as a major barrier to any hostile takeover.
Galileo never made a formal offer for the CWS but there has been widespread speculation that it is now "in play" with other parties interested in taking over parts of its varied empire.

"The nature of the City is that when you come up with an idea like this that does not go through, other people will try to take a similar path," a senior corporate financier told Reuters, adding that while others may be looking they might not strike.
No other bidders have yet emerged but Ireland's Allied Irish Banks said on Monday it would be interested in buying the Co-op Bank.
